speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The Government has implemented the Panel's recommendations since January 2016 based on the provisions within the current CPF Act.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Previously, members, including those below age 55, would have to set aside the Full Retirement Sum (FRS), which is twice the BRS, before they could make transfers to their spouses' accounts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We agreed with the CPF Advisory Panel to reduce the requirement from FRS to BRS so that more CPF members can make top-ups to their spouses' CPF savings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This flexibility will be useful for spouses who may not have enough CPF savings to join CPF LIFE for reasons, such as leaving the workforce earlier to take care of their children.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Both husband and wife can then have their own CPF LIFE plans and more secure retirement income for life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: When one spouse passes away, the surviving spouse will still be assured of lifelong payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As a family unit, both husband and wife can also maximise the extra interest earned on their combined CPF savings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 88 I encourage members to make full use of this flexibility to enhance their spouses' retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are also amending the CPF Act to state clearly that members will not be assessed for inclusion into the CPF LIFE scheme at age 55.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is because members now need to choose their CPF LIFE plan only when they reach their Payout Eligibility Age (PEA).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Hence, the previous requirement to select their CPF LIFE plan at age 55, which could be about 10 years before the start of payouts, is no longer necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Going forward, members will therefore need to be assessed for auto-inclusion into CPF LIFE only at their PEA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The second set of amendments relates to enhancing the insurance coverage under the CPF insurance schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: These are the Home Protection Scheme (HPS) and the Dependants' Protection Scheme (DPS).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, members can only make a claim from HPS and DPS in the event of death or incapacity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: By incapacity, it means that a member must not be able to ever continue in any form of employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This change will benefit new and existing persons insured under HPS and DPS, subject to the exclusions in their individual insurance covers arising from pre-existing conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I hope that this broader protection from our CPF insurance schemes will provide CPF members with greater peace of mind.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, insured members who have run out of Ordinary Account (OA) savings can only use their spouses' OA savings to pay for their HPS premiums if the spouse is a co-owner.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are now amending the CPF Act to allow such insured members to also use the OA savings of other co-owners, including children, parents or siblings, to help pay for their HPS premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: By allowing greater household support for the payment of HPS premiums, we can reduce the risk of lapsed insurance covers due to non-payment of HPS premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: More CPF members and their families will, therefore, be protected from losing their homes in the unfortunate event of death, permanent incapacity, terminal illness or total permanent disability.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, medical institutions and approved insurers help to facilitate the withdrawals from CPF member's MediSave accounts for approved treatments and uses under the MediSave Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In 2015, about $2.7 billion of MediSave savings was withdrawn.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Most medical institutions and approved insurers have made proper claims of MediSave monies and complied with our audit requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: However, a small number of medical institutions and approved insurers still make errors in some of their claims.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For example, in the past three years, we saw an average of about 40 cases a year of claims from wrong members' Page: 89 accounts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: These amendments will make medical institutions and approved insurers more accountable when they make claims of MediSave monies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The amended CPF Act will also mandate the recovery of any MediSave monies arising from unauthorised or wrongful deductions or uncompleted prepaid treatment packages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The first example is to revise the method of estimating the additional wages that attract CPF contributions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, employers are required to make an estimation based on the previous year's income.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are amending the CPF Act to allow employers to also make an estimation based on the projected wages in the current year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This amendment will improve efficiency as employers can estimate CPF liabilities more accurately, reducing the chances of employers overpaying CPF contributions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This will minimise the need for employers to apply for refunds for overpayments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This happens when the cheques were not cashed and subsequently expired.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The importance of mortgage insurance coverage struck close to home when I lost an uncle more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He passed away in a motorcycle accident and did not have any HPS coverage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A sizeable mortgage sum remained outstanding and it was left to my aunt and cousins to commit significant resources to continue making mortgage payments on top of their own commitments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At that time, I thought HPS non-coverage was a rare occurrence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But years later, it was heartbreaking to find out that some of my own residents, albeit a small number, found themselves in exactly the same position as my aunt and cousins when their sole breadwinner passes away Page: 90 unexpectedly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I wish to acknowledge the compassion shown by CPF and the Housing and Development Board (HDB) staff to try their best to assist affected families by retrospectively reinstating HPS coverage in certain cases so that the other family members do not face hardship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my last term, one particular family benefited from CPF's helpfulness and were profuse in their appreciation to me for pursuing the matter, but the appreciation should rightfully go to the agencies concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the 2014 Committee of Supply debate, I spoke on HPS, requesting the CPF to require HDB flat owners who are paying for their mortgage in cash to sign up for HPS as a matter of course.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More generally, the cut requested the Government to step up education on the importance of HPS, especially for low- to middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, the statistics pointed to an increase in the number of members who had lapsed in their HPS premium payments or who were no longer insurable for medical and other reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was 1.7% and 2% respectively in April 2011 and, by October 2013, the percentages had increased to 2% and 3%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I welcome the current amendments to allow co-owners, who could be family members, to help pay for HPS premiums, not just spouses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This should mitigate or reduce the number of lapsed policyholders going forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, for greater clarity, can the Minister give the House a primer on the regulations CPF has in mind in reinstating HPS insurance cover for paid claims when it is not liable to do so?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I welcome all the HPS-related amendments, I have three suggestions to make that could help strengthen HPS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2011, the CPF amendment modified the HPS scheme to allow for more portability, so that in the event the homeowner who purchased a new HDB flat was no longer in good health, he would remain insured under the scheme by way of earlier participation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This amendment acknowledges that a member in ill-health could yet be covered so as not to prejudice him or her.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the introduction of MediShield Life by the Government, a seminal change that differentiated it from the old MediShield scheme, was the inclusion of members with pre-existing conditions, albeit with a 30% increase in premiums payable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The philosophical basis of this move was in concert with making Singapore an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, HPS coverage for Singaporeans with pre-existing illnesses will buttress this in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government has raised its concerns about such an expansion, specifically on premium affordability in the past, and this is not an irrelevant consideration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, similar misgivings were overcome in the move from MediShield to MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This came up to almost $1.9 billion and with yet many thousands of other homeowners receiving less than the $400 but receiving a rebate nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The last time such rebates were paid out was in 2006.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In between, in 2011, HPS premiums were lowered by an average of 12% for some 80% of HPS members.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The remaining 20% were already paying low Page: 91 premiums.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With these numbers in mind, it would appear that there is some scope to relook at the prospect of covering members in poor health under HPS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Board can commit itself to look seriously to cover Singaporeans with pre-existing illnesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While HPS is compulsory for all members who use their CPF to pay for their HDB flats, subject to HDB's approval, members can choose to opt out should they take up a similar mortgage-reducing insurance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2015, it was made known that 43,610 flat owners had been given permission to do so by HDB.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, my understanding is that HDB does not monitor these members thereafter, allowing them to theoretically opt out of their mortgage-reducing insurance shortly thereafter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a case, these households effectively fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister confirm if CPF will consider plugging this hole in future and require them to sign up to HPS in the event their mortgage-reducing insurance lapses?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand CPF sends two reminder letters to the policyholder in the event of HPS premium non-payment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In an effort to highlight the importance of this scheme, can I confirm if these notifications are by ordinary post or registered mail?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, early reminders to the policyholders of low CPF balances for HPS premiums may be a powerful signalling tool that can prod members to top up their OA or, at the very least, seek assistance early, if they have other financial problems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the proposed amendments to the Bill in respect of HPS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: HPS is a mortgage-reducing insurance that protects members and their families against losing their homes in the event of death or permanent incapacity before their housing loans are paid up.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is compulsory for any HDB home owner who is using his or her CPF savings to pay the monthly housing loan instalments for his or her HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The scheme does not cover private residential properties, executive condominiums (ECs) or privatised Housing and Urban Development Company (HUDC) flats.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Buyers can only opt out of the scheme if they have taken a similar mortgage-reducing insurance policy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill seeks to enhance insurance coverage under HPS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this is a substantial change, it will Page: 92 represent a departure from the existing ruling under the current Act and it will be a welcomed change as it may provide more flexibility for members who are caught in different situations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: May the Minister please clarify whether this is what the Bill intended?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Bill provide for any other situation and where is this provided in the Bill?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Bill does not provide clearly for any other scenario, I am concerned that the Act may not be clear enough about the circumstances that may apply to the new situation where a CPF member who is insured under the scheme will now be allowed to make a claim under the scheme for terminal illness and total permanent disability, even though the member is not incapacitated from ever continuing in any employment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I seek the Minister's assurance that CPF Board will provide clear communication to CPF members for the circumstances which may apply under this proposed amendment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome this change as this recognises the possibility as well as perhaps the increasing occurrence of the situation where co-owners may not be spouses, for example, in the case of a flat which is owned by a man and his mother.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The change will address the current anomaly in the present Act.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: May the Minister clarify what would be these circumstances where the board may permit a member to join the scheme even though the Board may be aware of the member suffering from an illness at the time of joining the scheme?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister please confirm whether such members will still not be covered by the scheme after the amendment?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister consider allowing a special form of coverage under the scheme perhaps on a case-by-case basis and even on a different premium?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill also provides for regulations to be made to prescribe the circumstances where CPF Board may issue or reinstate an insurance cover or pay claims where the board is not liable to do so under sections 36(9) or (10).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: May the Minister please clarify the intention behind this proposed inclusion?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also support the amendments which allows the transfer of monies from the member's RA to another member's account for the purchase of an HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The amendments also allow CPF members to top up their spouse's RA or Special Account (SA) using money from their RA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This flexibility will benefit both the member and his/her spouse.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: CPF monies are, for many Singaporeans, a key source of funds and savings, and many seek greater flexibility on the withdrawal and use of the funds.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While recognising the need to allow for greater flexibility, with Singaporeans living longer, CPF funds remain an important source for a basic level of retirement funds.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amendments proposed provide for changes related to Part 1 of the CPF Advisory Panel's recommendations on enabling flexibility while ensuring retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But at the same time, I would say this is an extremely challenging balance to achieve.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Retirement Sum and the CPF LIFE plan are to meet the objective of giving members a monthly payout for life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Currently, subject to the amount of the CPF balances and the amount that they desire for monthly payouts, CPF Members have to make a choice of CPF LIFE plan − whether it is the LIFE Standard or the LIFE Basic Plan − when they turn 55 years of age.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The difference in the CPF LIFE plans is the monthly payouts you would receive and the amount you would bequest to the beneficiaries after you have passed on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I do welcome this change of not requiring members to make that decision on the choice of the CPF LIFE plan at the age of 55 as this is effectively 10 years before their PEA which is currently age 65.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Taking a decision closer to the date of the start of payouts will allow members to decide on the plan that best meets their retirement needs at the time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This change, while giving greater flexibility and enabling better decisions to meet retirement needs of members, however, does not address some of the concerns that members have with regard to PEA.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As PEA currently depends on your year of birth, this is not only confusing as to what your PEA is, there is also concern that this will continue to adjust for the subsequent age group of members.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This does cause uncertainty for members as PEA determines when you can start receiving your CPF LIFE payouts.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This gives a sense that access to CPF payouts is getting further delayed and can only be accessed when you get much older.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I understand the need to make the adjustments to be in line with people living longer and the standard of living, it is also important to give members some certainty.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Setting the expectations on previous PEAs, some members also – when they set the expectations, they kind of expect the payouts at that age – they feel misled that they had been expecting payouts at a certain age and, when that moves, it gets a little bit disappointing and, at other times, it leads to mistrust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, it would be good to understand the criteria for changing the PEA and what members can expect in the future for PEA.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed change also provides flexibility to allow for CPF members aged 55 and older, once they have set aside their BRS, to then transfer monies from their CPF accounts to their spouses’ RA or SA.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, this, until January this year, was twice the BRS.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, this change is definitely welcomed because it will help them help their spouses to grow their retirement savings, as well as to benefit from the extra interest on lower CPF balances.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This, as the Minister has pointed out, clearly will give the spouses better assurances of LIFE payouts for either of the Page: 94 spouses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, for older Singaporean women, this flexibility is important because, to receive top-ups from their spouses – as many of them have not accumulated as much CPF savings as men in that age group.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The changes proposed in the Bill of including terminal illness and total permanent disability as grounds for claims under HPS and DPS will allow members with terminal illness and total permanent disability to make claims on their HPS and DPS even when they are able to do some work, as the Minister has shared, although in a diminished capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I applaud this change as it not only enhances, but it really does give assurance to members as well as their families that they will have access and support when their family most need it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This additional flexibility will help to reduce the risk of lapsed insurance covers due to non-payment of premiums and this is especially so when members are facing financial challenges because this is exactly what they need, and home ownership, as we all know, is the key tenet for retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: HPS, as a mortgage-reducing insurance, gives members peace of mind that protects them and their families against losing their homes in the event of death or permanent incapacity before their housing loans are paid up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, as I have mentioned, those facing financial difficulties and, hence, perhaps will have challenges to keep up with their HPS payments with their OA savings being low, this change will allow them to get help from co-owners and not have them having to trade-off not paying the premium hence leading to a policy lapse.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have personally seen this happen when a family had their policy lapsed and they did not even know that the member had purchased HPS.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When he passed on, they then realised that he had actually lapsed on his policy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is quite sad because they still had to provide for the family.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That is the time when you need it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You are grieving and homeownership is one aspect.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If you had that addressed, that gives the remaining family members peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: MediSave – MediSave for many Singaporeans, is the fund for our and our immediate family's medical and future medical needs: hospitalisation, day surgery and other expenses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is, therefore important and I am glad that this change looks to safeguard members' MediSave monies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This uncertainty does lead to angst and mistrust of the scheme; and the irony of offering more choices Page: 95 in the usage of members' CPF monies is that it adds to the complexity of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To achieve simplicity is a very difficult balance, but CPF Board must continue to work on this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: CPF is and will continue to be an integral part of the retirement adequacy for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Ministry must continue to find effective channels to communicate and provide more timely and specific information to enable members to better understand the CPF schemes and changes as well as appropriate financial counselling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will ensure that members have a good understanding and can make informed choices that are best suited to each of their retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, on the issue of the HPS, I share the sentiments of the Members that it is very important that we do whatever we can to help to minimise the risk of losing a home when the home owner passes away.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the end of the day, it is very hard to keep a family together without a place to stay in.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, in that regard, we are very concerned that on the average every year, we see about 4,000 to 5,000 policyholders dropping out of HPS due to various reasons.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the part of the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and CPF, we are doing what we can to minimise or reduce these cases of lapses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having said so, we also continue to step up our efforts to remind and educate the homeowners of the importance of HPS.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about cases where we paid the HPS claims even though we are not liable to do so.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Here, I would like to give an illustration.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A policyholder fell sick; seriously ill and was hospitalised at the time when the premium payment was due.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, he was not able to take action, knowingly or unknowingly, to pay for the premium and, subsequently, he either passed away or suffered permanent disability.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, under such circumstances, CPF could have taken the position that since the policyholder did not pay for the premium, as a result, the policy has lapsed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But we think that will be a wrong thing to do because the fact that the policyholder was not able to pay the premium was beyond his control.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He was hospitalised at the time of the renewal.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, these are examples whereby the Board has exercised its judgement, knowing that if this is really beyond the control of the policyholder, in fact, we will find a way to pay them rather than to reject the claims.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked what kinds of serious illnesses would we exclude an application due to pre-existing illnesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, for a home owner who suffers from cancer, kidney failure or heart disorder and so on, the Board does look at the severity of the illness because if it is too severe and will lead clearly towards terminal illnesses, then I think we would have no choice but to reject such applications.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because at the end of the day, we would have to strike a balance between taking care of as many home owners as we can and yet, at the same time, be fair to the other home owners, bearing in mind that this is a risk-pooling programme.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Page: 96 Mr Pritam Singh also asked whether we can step up our efforts to send early reminders.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, today, not only would we remind every new home owner when they collect the keys from the HDB of the importance of HPS, we also make sure that for any case of a lapsed payment, we would follow up with a repeated reminder.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Obviously, more can be done; and we will keep doing more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked whether we can expand HPS to private housing.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For owners of private properties, our advice to them is to take care of themselves by purchasing mortgage-reducing insurance in the private market.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Tan asked whether we can be more specific with the definition of terminal illnesses and total permanent disability.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: All these are defined under the CPF Act and I would like to confirm that he is right that terminal illness, by and large, refers to a remaining lifespan of less than one year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of total permanent disability, it refers to a loss of two eyes, two limbs or one eye and one limb.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked for section 39 regarding premium with interest.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This refers to cases where the policyholder did not declare their serious pre-existing illnesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, at the time of claim, when it was discovered that the claim was not supportable, we will refund the remaining premium together with interest.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Jessica Tan touched on a few important points.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I share her concern that each time, when PEA is adjusted, it will affect the retirement planning of those CPF members who are affected.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And this is the reason why we take the review of PEA very seriously.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We phased in this increase of 62 to 65 over 10 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It was announced in 2007 that the final adjustment of going up from age 64 to 65 will only take place in 2018, which is about two years from now.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I agree with Ms Jessica Tan that this is a very major decision and should we decide to amend PEA, we should do so by giving policyholders and CPF members enough advance notice.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, I want to highlight to this House that since January this year, CPF members have the option of deferring the start of their CPF payouts from PEA up to the age of 70.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, if a CPF member is in employment and he does not need to start his payouts at the age of 64 now and 65 come 2018, he has the option of deferring the starting of his pay-out up to the age of 70.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe that the combination of progressively raising PEA to age 65 by 2018, coupled with the new flexibility of each member being able to, on a voluntary basis, defer the payout start age to 70, is about the right combination – providing the kind of flexibility that the members are looking for.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I also agree with Ms Jessica Tan regarding MediSave claims that are unauthorised or made by mistake.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last, but not least, Ms Jessica Tan also suggested stepping up our communications.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, CPF Board is not only going to do more; we are going to do more in a simpler way so that more members out there can understand what is the purpose of CPF, why it is structured this way and what are the changes that are coming along the way to ensure that the CPF system will always be relevant and able to meet their needs better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It is more of a clarification regarding the question I raised earlier, which maybe I did not make it clear.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I understand that under the current Act, people with certain pre-existing illnesses are not covered by the Act.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This presents a conundrum for members as it is normally compulsory for all members servicing their HDB loans through their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Can the Minister please confirm whether such members will merely be exempted from the scheme without any coverage from the scheme after the amendment?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Even if such members are exempted from the scheme, will the Minister consider allowing a special form of coverage under the scheme, perhaps on a case-by-case basis, and even perhaps on a different premium?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This will certainly give a better peace of mind to affected members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked whether they can be exempted.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, we encourage every home owner of HDB flats to come under HPS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think this question was contained in Mr Pritam Singh's speech which is that for members who are on HPS who fail to make the premium payments and reminder letters are sent to them, are these sent by registered mail or non-registered mail?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if they are sent by normal mail, could CPF Board give some thought to perhaps sending those reminders by registered mail?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: CPF Board does have regular communications with our members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, members who have recently received their CPF statement will see that CPF Board puts in tremendous efforts to provide a one-page summary of the status of all their transactions with CPF Board.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Obviously, we will keep looking for ways to improve our communications.
